# Round 63 §34 — the audited path, after the record was profiled.
# The ordinal and ceiling controls that lived here are GONE, and deliberately. They existed to size a
# code-model transformation of the audit call sites; §34 fixed the data structure that made those call
# sites look expensive, after which ordinal keys were SLOWER than the shipped path and the ceiling led
# by 3.6 ns on native alone. Neither is a configuration anyone should choose, so neither is a control
# worth defending. The measurements are kept in RECORDED-BASELINES; the bands are not.
# The §33 bands were recorded against a record with three faults in its hot path (an IdentityHashMap
# lookup per event, per-logger key caches, a resolved-once decision re-checked per entry). Fixing them
# moved the shipped arm 24% on JIT, so the old bands describe code that no longer exists. Retaken. These three arms differ ONLY in how a node reaches the record;
# records are byte-identical (188 B, one per event) and the graph checksum matches, which is asserted by
# the harness before a RESULT line is printed. Bands are the mean of three independent PGO builds +/-12%,
# wider than the other controls because the audited build lottery (+/-8 ns) is larger than the effect.
c-audit-noaudit
c-audit-noaudit
c-audit-string
c-audit-string
# C++ TARGET CONTROLS. Same discipline as the Java rows: fixed graph, fixed input, a checksum every arm
# must agree on. Two differences worth knowing:
#   1. $CPPB points at the output of cpp/build-controls.sh, which REBUILDS these from source. The Java
#      native rows point at a scratch directory and can only be re-run — if the machine is wiped they
#      are gone. These are not.
#   2. Bands are wider than the native Java ones. At sub-nanosecond the harness is near its limit: the
#      30-node arm was refused once at 2.23% batch spread before reading cleanly, so a tight band would
#      fail for measurement reasons rather than regressions.
# The number to watch is not any single row but c-cpp-conv against c-audit-noaudit-conv: that ratio is
# the C++ target's whole claim, and it is 2.8x today.
c-cpp-conv
# c-cpp-ladder (the four-node ladder, four separate nodes) is DELIBERATELY NOT A CONTROL. The harness
# refused it three times running at 2.23%, 2.57% and 2.83% batch spread against a 2% limit, while the
# other two C++ arms sit at 0.3% and 0.25% - so it is that arm, not the toolchain. A control whose
# reading the harness will not certify cannot detect a regression, because it cannot produce a number.
# Widening the limit to admit it would weaken the gate on the two arms that are well inside it.
# Its measurement lives in RECORDED-BASELINES; it is simply not gated.
c-cpp-ladder-fat
# AUDIT CONTROLS for the C++ target. c-cpp-audit-dense is the direct counterpart of c-audit-string:
# the same 30-node graph, every node logging, and — verified before the timing was believed — the same
# record SHAPE, 188 bytes per record. It was 172 until the C++ Tail was corrected to log both entries
# the Java one does; the checksum could not see that because it is computed on the graph's value, not
# on the log. avgRecBytes is what caught it, which is why the harness prints it.
c-cpp-audit-dense
c-cpp-audit-machinery
# The SAME graph (map -> map -> filter -> aggregate) emitted for BOTH targets by the generator, under
# LOWEST_LATENCY, no audit. Rebuild with dsl/build-dsl-controls.sh; every arm must checksum 488000000.
# The C++ arm is built at -O3, not -O2: measured 3.55 -> 2.76 ns, a 22% win against a prediction that
# -O2 had already inlined the templated chain. It had not. march=native and LTO are worth nothing, and
# PGO is 6% WORSE, so the control uses the flag that pays rather than every flag available.
# The Java native arm carries -H:-SpawnIsolates: without it native is SLOWER than JIT on this shape
# (11.04 against 10.42), which is the only graph in this kit where that holds. A deep chain of small
# flow-function objects is where the JVM's escape analysis earns its keep.
c-dsl
c-dsl
c-dsl
# M60 — the quote engine, the kit's only REPRESENTATIVE control. Six hand-written nodes doing what a
# quoting engine does, rather than two or three isolating one operator. Recorded 2026-09-10 by
# measure.sh, 3 batches x 5 reps, all four REPEATABLE at CV 0.37-0.60%, widened ~10% either side.
# Built by dsl/build-quoteengine-controls.sh, which REFUSES to build an arm that emits any guard: the
# engine's claim is straight-line dispatch, and a build that quietly reinstated dirty flags would still

# All four arms are ALLOCATION-FREE, each checked a different way: the JVM's per-thread accounting
# reads 0 bytes/event, both Java arms run 25M events under a NON-COLLECTING GC on a 32MB heap, and the
# C++ arms report heapCalls=0 from a counting global operator new.
qe-java-plain
qe-java-audit
